title: Infra GPU Fleet Capacity, Cloud Accounts & Networking IaC/CI-CD Playbook (2026 ops)
author: Marina Kovács
content:
Overview

Summary
This playbook consolidates infrastructure engineering standards and runbooks for Redwood's GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD pipelines. It is intended for infra engineers, on-call SREs, and platform owners. The document combines design patterns, operational runbooks, sample Terraform modules and CI job snippets, and escalation/playback steps for common failure modes.

Scope
- Applies to hosted (public) and Dedicated/private GPU pools, cloud accounts in AWS/GCP, and on-prem reference patterns.
- Covers Terraform module standards, CI/CD pipelines for infra changes, capacity planning thresholds, autoscaling policies, and networking configuration required by inference services.

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-gpu-pool@redwood (team: infrastructure)
- Secondary owner: eng-sre-oncall@redwood
- Architects: Marina Kovács (author), Diego Rivera
- Pager: infra-oncall rotation (see oncall roster)

Key SLOs and capacity objectives
- Serving latency SLO: 99th percentile <= 150 ms per token for interactive routes (measured at gateway).
- Fleet availability target: 99.9% (excl. planned maintenance).
- Scale-up time objective: new node available and drained into load balancer within 3 minutes for autoscale events.
- Buffer capacity: maintain a min-headroom of 15% of peak 7-day rolling usage to absorb spikes.

Capacity planning and forecasting
1. Data sources
   - Prometheus metrics: gpu_utilization, request_rate_per_model, queue_length
   - Billing + usage: daily per-customer token counts from the API billing pipeline
   - Job and batch schedules: nightly retraining and eval windows
2. Forecast cadence
   - Weekly: 7-day rolling peak and headroom report (generated by infra-ops job)
   - Quarterly: capacity planning meeting with product and sales to convert pipeline to commit capacity
3. Thresholds and actions
   - If peak utilization > 80% sustained for 12 hours -> open capacity ticket and trigger scale-up plan
   - If headroom < 10% -> enable burst pool (if available) and notify sales/cs for rate-limit guidance

GPU pool topology and node types
- Node pools by workload:
  - interactive-general: H100-80GB (preferred), target for low-latency chat endpoints
  - batch-inference: A100-80GB (cost-effective), scheduled for large-batch jobs and evals
  - quantized-cost: T4/GPU-optimized lower-cost nodes for 8-bit quantized models
- Pool tagging: tag resources with "team:service", "env:prod|staging|dev", and "gpu_pool:<name>" for billing and ownership

Networking & cloud accounts (high level)
- VPCs: Each environment (prod/staging/dev) has a separate VPC. Prod VPCs are peered with private control plane endpoints for Dedicated customers.
- Subnets: split by AZ with private subnets for compute and separate management subnets for bastions and jump hosts.
- Egress: use NAT gateways with per-account egress logging; large model downloads go through signed artifact proxy.
- Security groups: minimum-privilege SGs; only allow service mesh and orchestration control-plane ports.
- Cross-account setup: shared-network account holds Transit Gateway and centralized logging; compute accounts consume via AWS Resource Access Manager.

Terraform / IaC standards
- Module naming and layout
  - Module: redwood-gpu-node-pool
    - Usage: single module per node pool, param-driven for gpu_type, instance_type, autoscaler config
  - Modules must be documented with variables and outputs and include example usage in /examples
- State and secrets
  - Remote state: S3 backend with state locking (DynamoDB) and kms encryption
  - Secrets: use dedicated KMS keys per account; store transient API tokens in Vault
- Review and change policy
  - All TF changes through PR in infra repo, pass linting (tflint), plan approval via CI, and a staged apply pipeline

Sample Terraform module snippet
```
module "gpu_pool_interactive" {
  source        = "git::ssh://repo.redwood/infra-modules.git//modules/redwood-gpu-node-pool"
  name          = "interactive-general"
  gpu_type      = "h100"
  instance_type = "p5.48xlarge"
  min_size      = 2
  max_size      = 100
  autoscaler = {
    scale_out_threshold = 0.75
    scale_in_threshold  = 0.30
    cooldown_seconds    = 180
  }
  tags = {
    team = "inference"
    env  = "prod"
  }
}
```

CI/CD pipelines for infra changes
- Pipeline stages (infra repo):
  1. Lint (tflint, terraform fmt)
  2. Static security checks (checkov/policy)
  3. Plan (terraform plan against non-prod remote state)
  4. Manual approval for prod plans (engineering leads)
  5. Apply (staged: canary apply to a single AZ/node pool -> full apply)

Example GitLab job for plan step
```
plan:
  stage: plan
  image: hashicorp/terraform:1.4.6
  script:
    - terraform init -backend-config="bucket=$TF_STATE_BUCKET"
    - terraform fmt -check
    - terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - plan.tfplan
```

Runbook: common incidents and remediation
- Incident type: autoscaler failing to scale up
  - Symptoms: queue_length rising; model latency increases; alerts: cpu_utilization > 85% and pending_pods > 0
  - Immediate actions:
    1. Acknowledge pager and post to #infra-oncall with incident tag
    2. Check autoscaler controller logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/hpa-controller
    3. Verify cloud API quotas and spot capacity for instance type
    4. If quota exhausted: open cloud support ticket and enable fallback pool (quantized-cost)
    5. If controller crashed: restart deployment (kubectl rollout restart)
  - Recovery validation: confirm queue length reduces and p99 latency returns to baseline within 30 minutes
- Incident type: terraform apply failures in prod
  - Symptoms: plan succeeded but apply errors with IAM or quota
  - Immediate actions:
    1. Abort apply if partial (terraform apply interruption may leave partial resources)
    2. Re-run plan with debug logs and check provider rate limits
    3. If IAM error: check recent policy changes in the security account and rollback PR
    4. Restore state from prior known-good with state locking coordination

Operational dashboards and alerts (examples)
- Dashboards:
  - GPU Fleet Overview: total GPUs, utilization by pool, queued requests, average start-up time
  - Network egress and artifact download latencies
  - Terraform pipeline health: recent plan/apply success rates
- Alerts (Pager thresholds):
  - high-gpu-utilization: any pool 95%+ for 10m -> P1 page to infra-oncall
  - autoscaler-errors: controller error rate > 5% in 5m -> P1
  - missing-headroom: headroom < 5% for 30m -> P2

Change windows and maintenance
- Regular maintenance: weekly rolling updates in staging; monthly maintenance window for prod (first Sunday 02:00-06:00 UTC)
- Emergency changes: require follow-up postmortem and config freeze lift approval from infra lead

Playbook checklist (pre-deploy)
- Run terraform fmt and tflint locally
- Ensure unit tests and integration tests in CI pass
- Verify plan diff includes only intended resources
- Coordinate with product for capacity-impacting changes
- Notify oncall and schedule canary apply

Post-deploy verification
- Confirm new instances are Registered and Ready in the pool
- Verify health checks and readiness probes are green
- Confirm SLO metrics for sample requests across AZs

Appendix: useful commands
- Check node pool autoscaler status
  kubectl -n infra get hpa -l pool=interactive-general -o wide
- Inspect terraform remote state
  aws s3 cp s3://tf-state-prod/infra/terraform.tfstate - | jq '.resources[] | select(.type=="aws_instance")'
- Force a rolling restart of the node pool (AWS ASG example)
  aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name redwood-gpu-interactive --preferences '"InstanceWarmup": 180'
